# Rule catalog: patterns x engines

<!-- GENERATED by scripts/render_catalog.py from src/catalog/ -- do not edit. -->

Generated from `src/catalog/engines/*.toml`, `src/catalog/patterns/*.toml`, `src/catalog/routing.toml`, `src/catalog/gates.toml` and `src/catalog/triage_signals.toml` (ADR-031 Decision 8). Change a TOML file, then run `uv run python scripts/render_catalog.py`. Field definitions: `src/shared/catalog/engines.py`, `src/shared/catalog/patterns.py` and `src/shared/catalog/routing.py`.

**Compatibility.** The TOML format (file locations, table and key names, value types, which keys are required) is backwards compatible within 0.x: a release may add keys and files, but does not remove, rename or retype one without a documented deprecation first (`tests/contract/catalog_format_snapshot.json`, #1647). Rule ids (the engine, pattern, gap rule and write intent files, and named entries such as thresholds and signals) are stable; retiring one needs a deprecation. The values on this page (scores, penalties, prices, thresholds) are routing tuning and change between releases; each release's notes list the values that moved. Read them from the catalog files; do not hard-code them.

## Score weights

How each engine weighs a query's four score dimensions (ADR-031 Decision 5), from its `[score_weights.<profile>]` tables; the first profile is the engine's default, and an engine with none uses the default split. Every engine gives cost the same weight (#1002).

| Engine | Profile | Pattern match | Complexity | Performance | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | default | 64% | 21% | 5% | 10% |
| DocumentDB | default | 48% | 26% | 16% | 10% |
| OpenSearch | search | 45% | 25% | 20% | 10% |
| OpenSearch | time_series | 40% | 20% | 30% | 10% |
| Aurora PostgreSQL | default | 40% | 30% | 20% | 10% |
| Aurora MySQL | default | 40% | 30% | 20% | 10% |
| Any other engine | default | 40% | 30% | 20% | 10% |

## Engine routing properties

From each engine file: the source engines whose own dialect it is, whether it scores a query only on the query's own matched pattern, what the reality check lets it absorb, whether a signal override onto it needs the justification floor, and the complexity points for 1, 2, ... feature patterns.

| Engine | Source engines | Pattern only | Absorbs only | Override needs justification | Complexity by feature count |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | - | no | - | no | - |
| DocumentDB | - | no | - | no | - |
| OpenSearch | - | yes | signal `text_search`, signal `aggregations`, capability `text_pattern_match` | yes | - |
| ElastiCache | - | no | - | no | - |
| Aurora PostgreSQL | `postgresql`, `postgres` | no | - | no | 10, 15 |
| Aurora MySQL | `mysql`, `mariadb` | no | - | no | 10, 15 |

Engine-specific routing rules, each an engine-file field the routing code reads instead of naming the engine (#1081):

| Engine | Rule |
|---|---|
| DynamoDB | a join consolidated away from engines none of which is relational or flagged like this one never lands here (it needs a denormalised design) |
| OpenSearch | justification floor `search_depth` (ledger reason `floor.opensearch`): A standing search domain earns a query only with real search depth (relevance ranking, fuzzy matching or a facet) and enough traffic or result size to pay for it (#326). |
| Aurora PostgreSQL | wins an exact heterogeneous Aurora tie no feature breaks, by maintainer rule (ADR-031 Decision 6 Amendment 1): a named-engine preference held as data |

The source features that tip a close or tied heterogeneous Aurora call (`routing.toml`, ADR-031 Decision 6): the choice counts the features on each side, the workload ones first and the dialect ones only when no workload feature decides.

| Feature | Favours | Basis | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sequences` | Aurora PostgreSQL | workload | Sequences (CREATE SEQUENCE, NEXT VALUE FOR, NEXTVAL) map onto PostgreSQL sequences; MySQL has none and needs AUTO_INCREMENT or a table emulation (#381). |
| `merge_statements` | Aurora PostgreSQL | workload | MERGE runs on PostgreSQL 15 and later; MySQL has no MERGE and needs INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE rewrites (#381). |
| `json_usage` | Aurora PostgreSQL | workload | JSON columns and functions map onto PostgreSQL's jsonb with its indexes and operators more directly than onto MySQL's JSON type (#381; both engines store JSON, so this direction is under review in #445). |
| `multiple_schemas` | Aurora PostgreSQL | workload | Several schemas in one database map onto PostgreSQL schemas; in MySQL a schema is a database, so they split into several (#381). |
| `babelfish_compatible` | Aurora PostgreSQL | dialect | Babelfish, the SQL Server wire-protocol and T-SQL compatibility layer, exists only for Aurora PostgreSQL; every SQL Server source reports it, so it decides only when no workload feature does (#381; maintainer decision recorded on #445). |

## Thresholds

The routing thresholds and floors: shared ones from `src/catalog/routing.toml`, an engine's own from its file's `[thresholds.<name>]`.

| Applies to | Threshold | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Every engine | `small_reference_table_max_rows` | 10000 | A table with at most this many collected rows is small reference data: read whole, it is the reference-read class (ADR-031 Decision 14 Amendment 7, #920), the limit DynamoDB's metadata-config-store reads, and a whole read of it is a scan a redesign removes, by caching or keeping it as one item collection (ADR-031 Decision 2 Amendment 13, #1231). |
| Every engine | `redesign_key_min_distinct` | 100 | A column needs at least this many collected distinct values before a redesign may assume a key on it from its statistics (ADR-031 Decision 2 Amendment 13, #1231): fewer values address a few large slices of the table, not entities, whatever their share of the rows. |
| Every engine | `redesign_key_min_rows` | 10000 | Statistics overrule a category name or type (a status, a type) only on a table with at least this many collected rows (#1231): on a smaller table almost any distinct count clears the 1% low-cardinality share, so the count says nothing about whether the column addresses entities; the small reference-table limit, the same 10,000. |
| Every engine | `target_engine_count` | 2 | The reality check tries to stay at or below this many target engines; a third must provide unique, irreplaceable capabilities (ADR-031 Decision 7). |
| Every engine | `unique_delta_threshold` | 15 | Points by which an engine must beat the best alternative for a query to count as unique to it; within this margin the query is redundant (reality check differentiation). |
| Every engine | `mandatory_engine_cost_floor` | 100 | Fixed monthly cost (USD) an engine kept by a signal override must reach before its workload share is questioned: DynamoDB ($0) and ElastiCache ($50) are cheap enough that a small share is not disproportionate (#167). |
| Every engine | `mandatory_engine_max_query_share` | 0.05 | Share of in-scope queries below which a mandatory engine's fixed cost counts as disproportionate to the workload it serves (#167). |
| Every engine | `cheaper_engine_min_saving_share` | 0.4 | An engine that scores the source-compatible engine's queries no better replaces it only when at least this much cheaper in standing cost, as a share of the source-compatible engine's cost, inclusive (maintainer decision on #600, ADR-031 Decision 13). |
| Every engine | `cheaper_engine_min_saving_monthly` | 100 | ... and only when it also saves at least this much a month (USD), inclusive (maintainer decision on #600, ADR-031 Decision 13). |
| Every engine | `orphan_engine_threshold` | 5 | An engine left with this many queries or fewer (and no hard capability requirement) is a candidate for the reality check's sanity sweep redirect. |
| Every engine | `aurora_choice_margin_ratio` | 0.05 | For a heterogeneous source, Aurora totals within this share of the larger one are close enough for source features to decide; on the reference samples both Aurora engines scored byte-identically (#381, ADR-031 Decision 6). |
| OpenSearch | `min_calls_per_second` | 1 | Combined calls/s across every query OpenSearch would own before its fixed cost is worth a standing domain: the cache overlay's hot-read floor, the lowest traffic worth a dedicated store (#326). |
| OpenSearch | `native_override_min_calls_per_second` | 10 | The floor when the source engine's own text search (MySQL FULLTEXT, PostgreSQL tsvector or pg_trgm) already serves the pattern: ten times the base floor, since that index is already paid for (#326). |
| OpenSearch | `min_corpus_rows_avg` | 1000 | Average rows a query returns that marks a corpus large enough for a dedicated index to earn its cost below the traffic floor; a result-size proxy, the only per-query signal the collector gives (#326). |
| ElastiCache | `hot_read_min_calls_per_second` | 1 | Hot-read floor, inclusive: below one call/s a cached entry is read a few times before the next miss pays the same cost as no cache (#296); on the reference samples every candidate is at least 1.26 calls/s or at most 0.95. |
| ElastiCache | `max_rows_avg` | 100 | Largest average result (rows) a cached query may return: a cache holds bounded values (#296). |
| ElastiCache | `write_heavy_table_min_write_share` | 0.5 | A table whose writes are at least this share of its calls is write-heavy: its cache entries would be invalidated about as often as they are read (#296). |

## Hard gates

From `src/catalog/gates.toml` (ADR-031 Decision 2 steps 2 and 3). An engine without a capability cannot serve a query that needs it: one showing a listed query fact or triage signal. A capability linked to a pattern capability names the same engines as those pattern files' `supported` flags (the loader checks it).

| Capability | Engines | Query facts | Triage signals | Pattern capability | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `multi_doc_acid` | DynamoDB, DocumentDB, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | structural | - | `acid_transactions` | Multi-item ACID writes. DynamoDB's TransactWriteItems/TransactGetItems are ACID across up to 100 items (ADR-031 Decision 3); a write too wide for one transaction is scored by its shape (wide-transaction, #493). Detected structurally, not from the query text. |
| `strong_consistency` | DynamoDB, DocumentDB, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | structural | - | - | Strongly consistent reads. No query fact requires it today. |
| `aggregation` | DocumentDB, OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | `needs_aggregation` | `aggregations` | - | An aggregate call, SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS, a window function, or a GROUP BY that does more than de-duplicate (#336, #338): an engine with no aggregation (DynamoDB) cannot run it at all, even on a single query. |
| `text_pattern_match` | DocumentDB, OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | `text_search` | `text_search` | `text_search` | A text-pattern predicate (a leading-wildcard or parameterised LIKE, a full-text, regular-expression or similarity match, #893). DocumentDB runs it with $regex and $text (#485); a leading-wildcard predicate that runs as a scan is a score difference (substring-match), never this gate. |
| `scan_engine` | OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | `recursive_cte` | - | - | A recursive CTE (a ranking or offset window function before #968, now their own capabilities). |
| `ranking_window` | DocumentDB, OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | `ranking_window_function` | - | - | ROW_NUMBER, RANK or DENSE_RANK over a window. DocumentDB runs them with $setWindowFields ($documentNumber, $rank, $denseRank) on 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster: a version bound the window-functions anti-pattern prices, not a capability gap (#968; Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types). |
| `offset_window` | OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | `offset_window_function` | - | - | LAG, LEAD or NTILE over a window: it reads another row or buckets rows. DocumentDB cannot run them on any version: LAG and LEAD need $shift, which no version supports, and the supported operators include no bucketing window operator for NTILE (#968; Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types). |
| `complex_joins` | Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | structural | `complex_joins` | - | Joins of three or more tables: DynamoDB and OpenSearch have no join, however the data is keyed (#338). |
| `sql_admin` | Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | structural | - | - | A utility or metadata statement (DDL, session variables, transaction control, #327): only the Aurora engines understand it. Detected by utility_statements, not a query fact. |
| `computed_join` | Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL | `computed_join_key` | - | - | A join on a computed expression (lower(g.name) = u.username_lower), which a key lookup cannot evaluate (review of #375, finding B2). |

Exclusions, checked in order: the engine cannot serve a query showing the fact.

| Engine | Rule | Fact | Why (technical) | What a rejected override says |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | `ddb-no-leading-wildcard` | `leading_wildcard_like` | Leading wildcard LIKE '%term' requires full scan; search engine territory | uses a leading-wildcard search (LIKE '%...') |
| OpenSearch | `os-no-write-subquery` | `write_with_subquery` | OpenSearch cannot perform transactional writes with subquery logic. The application layer must handle conditional insert/update logic before indexing. | performs a conditional write with a subquery, which needs transactional guarantees it can't provide |
| ElastiCache | `ec-no-complex-join` | `join_count` >= 2 | ElastiCache cannot perform multi-table JOINs; it's a key-value/data structure store | joins more than one table, and a key-value store can't serve joins |

Waivers (ADR-031 Decision 2 Amendment 12): the engine serves a capability it lacks for a query showing the class fact, when the condition holds. The shared scorer still decides whether the engine wins.

| Engine | Rule | Capability | Class fact | When | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | `ddb-key-scoped-count` | `aggregation` | `key_scoped_count` | the query's table has its source of truth (its writes) on the engine | A COUNT with no GROUP BY over the rows one key value of one table addresses is a DynamoDB Query on that key with Select = COUNT, which returns the number of matching items (after any filter expression; a COUNT(col) adds attribute_exists(col)) instead of the items, yet still reads and bills every matching item: read capacity is the same as reading them, and a result past 1 MB is paged, so the count is summed over the pages (Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Query, Select; maintainer decision on #377). It applies only when the table's writes are on DynamoDB, so no table is pulled off another engine for one count; routing has no cardinality gate, so the DynamoDB designer is given each such count's key and its cardinality (or unknown) to choose the key or a maintained counter. MIN and MAX are not waived (they need a designed sort key). |

## Pattern x engine matrix

Each cell is what a query showing the pattern gets on that engine: `fit N` (the engine's analysis reports it, catalog score N), `fit (level)` (reported with a confidence level instead of a score), `anti S` (reported as an anti-pattern, severity S), `native` (has the capability, never penalised), `scan` (lacks it and runs the pattern as a scan: loses the pattern's penalty only on a query that crosses its scan threshold), `redesign -N` (lacks it, bounded redesign, N-point penalty), **no** (cannot run it: takes the full penalty when another engine reports it as a fit), `no` (cannot run it, no score effect; `anti S, no` for a reported anti-pattern), `-` (no effect) or `future` (a future-enhancement placeholder: not modelled yet, never a routing candidate). Penalty is the points lost on an engine that reports it as an anti-pattern, or on every other engine when one reports it as a fit. One rule sizes it (ADR-031 Decision 8 Amendment 6): the penalty basis, the consequence the engines' public documentation states for the pattern, fixes the points (`cannot_run` 40, `needs_redesign` 30, `reads_more_than_returns` 20, `workload_fit` 20, `bounded_limit` 10, `guidance_only` 0).

## Patterns

### acid-transactions

Name: ACID transactions.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.opensearch_analysis_tools:analyze_opensearch_use_cases`.

- DynamoDB, native: TransactWriteItems/TransactGetItems are ACID across up to 100 items, and a conditional write is ACID on one item; a wider write is scored by its shape \(wide-transaction\).
- DocumentDB, native: Multi-document ACID transactions are native \(engine 4.0 or later, one-minute limit per transaction\).
- OpenSearch, anti 0.6, no (os-ap-02): Frequent UPDATE/DELETE operations \(&gt; 1 CPS\) indicate mutable data with ACID transactional requirements. OpenSearch has no multi-document transactions: each document write stands alone \(OpenSearch documentation, Bulk API\).
- Aurora PostgreSQL, native: Multi-statement, multi-table ACID transactions \(BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK\) are native.
- Aurora MySQL, native: Multi-statement, multi-table ACID transactions \(BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK\) are native.
- No effect on: ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### adjacency-list

Name: Adjacency list.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.dynamodb_analysis_tools:analyze_dynamodb_use_cases`.

- DynamoDB, fit 60 (dynamodb-07d): Hierarchical or graph-like relationship \(self-referential FK or multi-level hierarchy traversal\). Maps to DynamoDB adjacency list pattern with PK/SK design. Table bonus: +5 pattern match, -10 complexity (once for the `denormalizable-join` group).
- No effect on: DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### aggregation-analytics

Name: Aggregation analytics.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 85 (aurora-common-02): Aggregation queries with GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregate functions \(SUM, COUNT, AVG\). Aurora handles analytical aggregations efficiently with parallel query execution.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 85 (aurora-common-02): Aggregation queries with GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregate functions \(SUM, COUNT, AVG\). Aurora handles analytical aggregations efficiently with parallel query execution.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### aggregation-pipeline

Name: Aggregation pipeline.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, fit 75 (documentdb-05): A grouped aggregate, or one over rows no key anchors, that maps to DocumentDB's aggregation pipeline \($group, $match, $project, $sort\). Table bonus: +8 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### array-operations

Name: Array operations.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_pg_analysis_tools:detect_pg_specific_features`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 80 (aurora-pg-04): Array operations \(ANY, array\_agg, unnest\) for multi-value attributes. Aurora PG handles array containment queries with GIN indexes, avoiding junction tables for simple multi-value cases. Counts toward the engine's feature complexity bonus.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### audit-columns-only

Name: Audit columns only.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.opensearch_analysis_tools:analyze_opensearch_use_cases`.

- OpenSearch, anti 0.1 (os-ap-03): Timestamp columns \(created\_at, updated\_at, event\_time, etc.\) used only in equality checks, not range queries. This is an audit/metadata pattern, not a time-series workload. Guard rail to prevent false time-series classification; guidance only, since no OpenSearch limit applies \(OpenSearch documentation, Date field type\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### batch-in-list

Name: Batch IN list.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 70 (aurora-common-11): Batch lookups using WHERE column IN \(...\) with multiple values: one index scan probes every listed value \(PostgreSQL documentation, Indexes, a ScalarArrayOpExpr on a B-tree; MySQL Reference Manual, Range Optimization, equality ranges for IN lists\), with no item limit, where DynamoDB's BatchGetItem takes at most 100 keys and 16 MB \(Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, BatchGetItem\). In the key-lookup class it raises no score: key-value-lookup rates the same read at 80.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 70 (aurora-common-11): Batch lookups using WHERE column IN \(...\) with multiple values: one index scan probes every listed value \(PostgreSQL documentation, Indexes, a ScalarArrayOpExpr on a B-tree; MySQL Reference Manual, Range Optimization, equality ranges for IN lists\), with no item limit, where DynamoDB's BatchGetItem takes at most 100 keys and 16 MB \(Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, BatchGetItem\). In the key-lookup class it raises no score: key-value-lookup rates the same read at 80.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### bounded-parent-child

Name: Bounded parent-child.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.dynamodb_analysis_tools:analyze_dynamodb_use_cases`.

- DynamoDB, fit 75 (dynamodb-07a): Parent-child relationship where the cardinality can be reasoned about at design time. A partition key value's item collection has no size limit unless the table has a local secondary index \(then 10 GB\). The bound is domain-driven \(e.g., order → items, user → addresses\) \(Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Local secondary indexes\). Large item collections may need creative sort key design for efficient range queries. Table bonus: +5 pattern match, -10 complexity (once for the `denormalizable-join` group).
- No effect on: DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### caching

Name: Caching.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.redis_analysis_tools:analyze_redis_use_cases`.

- ElastiCache, fit (high) (redis-caching-001): Detected high-frequency SELECT queries suitable for caching
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### co-accessed-tables

Name: Co-accessed tables.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.dynamodb_analysis_tools:analyze_dynamodb_use_cases`.

- DynamoDB, fit 70 (dynamodb-07c): Tables frequently accessed together in the same queries \(co-access frequency &gt; 50 calls/hour\). Strong signal for denormalization into one item collection that a single Query returns \(Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Best practices for modeling relational data\). Table bonus: +5 pattern match, -10 complexity (once for the `denormalizable-join` group).
- No effect on: DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### complex-aggregation

Name: Complex aggregation.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.dynamodb_analysis_tools:analyze_dynamodb_use_cases`.

- DynamoDB, anti 0.7 (dynamodb-ap-02): GROUP BY, HAVING, or an aggregate over rows no key anchors or over a join \(one key's COUNT or SUM is a Query on that key, not this pattern\). DynamoDB has no server-side aggregation: a Query or Scan can only count the items it reads \(Select = COUNT\), so a grouped result needs the application layer, pre-computed aggregates or a separate analytics store \(Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, Query\).
- No effect on: DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### complex-join

Name: Complex join.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 90 (aurora-common-01): Queries joining 3+ tables with multiple join conditions. Aurora's query optimizer excels at complex join planning: hash joins, merge joins, and nested loop selection are automatic and performant at scale.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 90 (aurora-common-01): Queries joining 3+ tables with multiple join conditions. Aurora's query optimizer excels at complex join planning: hash joins, merge joins, and nested loop selection are automatic and performant at scale.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### correlated-subquery-joins

Name: Correlated subquery joins.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, anti 0.7 (documentdb-anti-08): Queries with correlated subqueries. A correlated $lookup \(let/pipeline\) runs its sub-pipeline for each input document, and needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types\); otherwise pre-denormalize.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### correlated-subquery

Name: Correlated subquery.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 80 (aurora-common-06): Correlated subqueries using EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, or IN \(SELECT ...\). Aurora's optimizer can decorrelate and flatten these into efficient join plans.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 80 (aurora-common-06): Correlated subqueries using EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, or IN \(SELECT ...\). Aurora's optimizer can decorrelate and flatten these into efficient join plans.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### cte-recursive

Name: Recursive CTE.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_pg_analysis_tools:detect_pg_specific_features`, `src.tools.analysis.aurora_mysql_analysis_tools:detect_mysql_specific_features`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 95 (aurora-pg-01): Recursive CTEs \(WITH RECURSIVE\) for hierarchical data traversal: org charts, category trees, bills of materials, with the SEARCH and CYCLE clauses for traversal order and cycle detection and no default recursion limit \(PostgreSQL documentation, WITH Queries\). Table bonus: +15 pattern match. Counts toward the engine's feature complexity bonus.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 90 (aurora-mysql-08): Recursive CTEs \(WITH RECURSIVE\) for hierarchical data traversal on MySQL 8.0, which Aurora MySQL version 3 is compatible with; recursion stops at cte\_max\_recursion\_depth \(1000 by default\) and there is no SEARCH or CYCLE clause, so cycles are guarded in the query \(MySQL Reference Manual, WITH \(Common Table Expressions\)\). Table bonus: +15 pattern match. Counts toward the engine's feature complexity bonus.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### extended-reference

Name: Extended reference.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, fit 85 (documentdb-07): Queries joining large transactional tables with small reference/lookup tables \(country, merchant, payment\_type\) just to get display names. Embed the few referenced fields directly, especially valuable in DocumentDB, where every $lookup is a read-time join. Table bonus: +10 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### faceted-analytics

Name: Faceted analytics.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, anti 0.5 (documentdb-anti-06): Several groupings of one row set in one statement \(GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE\): $facet runs them in one pipeline on DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types\). A GROUP BY over several columns is one $group with a compound \_id, native on every version, and is not this pattern.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### frequent-full-scan

Name: Frequent full scan.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.dynamodb_analysis_tools:analyze_dynamodb_use_cases`.

- DynamoDB, anti 0.5 (dynamodb-ap-01): A read more frequent than once a minute that pins no column to a value, so no partition key value can address it whatever the key design. On DynamoDB that is a Scan, which reads every item and consumes read capacity for every item it reads, not only the ones it returns \(Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Scanning tables\).
- No effect on: DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### full-text-native

Name: PostgreSQL native full-text search.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_pg_analysis_tools:detect_pg_specific_features`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 75 (aurora-pg-05): Native full-text search using to\_tsvector, ts\_query, and @@ operator. Aurora PG provides built-in full-text with GIN indexes, suitable for moderate search workloads without a separate search engine. Table bonus: +10 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### full-text-search-candidate

Name: Full-text search with LIKE.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, anti 0.6 (aurora-anti-03): Full-text search patterns using LIKE '%term%' or similar constructs. Guidance only: the scan an unindexed substring match needs is priced once, as its own pattern, and a word search is not penalised \(PostgreSQL documentation, pg\_trgm\).
- Aurora MySQL, anti 0.6 (aurora-anti-03): Full-text search patterns using LIKE '%term%' or similar constructs. Guidance only: the scan an unindexed substring match needs is priced once, as its own pattern, and a word search is not penalised \(PostgreSQL documentation, pg\_trgm\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### full-text-search

Name: Full-text search.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.opensearch_analysis_tools:analyze_opensearch_use_cases`.
Exemption note: {engine} runs this search pattern natively: not penalized. OpenSearch is worth the move only when traffic, data size or search depth justify a dedicated search engine

- DynamoDB, no: DynamoDB cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on DynamoDB.
- DocumentDB, native, class score 60: The $text operator runs full-text search natively within its documented limits: one text index per collection, English only, no array fields, no compound index with other fields and no term exclusion \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Performing text search\). Class score \(#728\): 60, a narrow text index, not a search engine.
- OpenSearch, fit 95 (os-01): Full-text search using PostgreSQL tsvector/tsquery operators or MySQL MATCH AGAINST. OpenSearch's inverted index is purpose-built for this workload: tokenization, stemming, and relevance ranking are native. Table bonus: +15 pattern match.
- ElastiCache, no: ElastiCache cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on ElastiCache.
- Aurora PostgreSQL, native, class score 75: tsvector and tsquery full-text search with a GIN index is native SQL \(PostgreSQL documentation, Full Text Search, Preferred Index Types for Text Search\). Class score \(#728\): 75, a built-in text index for moderate search, below a dedicated search engine's relevance ranking.
- Aurora MySQL, native, class score 80: FULLTEXT indexes with MATCH ... AGAINST, in natural-language and boolean modes, are native SQL \(MySQL Reference Manual, Full-Text Search Functions\). Class score \(#728\): 80, a built-in text index for moderate search, below a dedicated search engine's relevance ranking.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### fulltext-search

Name: MySQL FULLTEXT search.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_mysql_analysis_tools:detect_mysql_specific_features`.

- Aurora MySQL, fit 80 (aurora-mysql-02): Full-text search using MATCH ... AGAINST with FULLTEXT indexes. Aurora MySQL provides built-in boolean and natural language full-text modes suitable for moderate search workloads. Table bonus: +10 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### fuzzy-search

Name: Fuzzy search.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.opensearch_analysis_tools:analyze_opensearch_use_cases`.
Exemption note: {engine} runs this search pattern natively: not penalized. OpenSearch is worth the move only when traffic, data size or search depth justify a dedicated search engine

- DynamoDB, no: DynamoDB cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on DynamoDB.
- DocumentDB, no: DocumentDB cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on DocumentDB.
- OpenSearch, fit 85 (os-04): Fuzzy/similarity search via pg\_trgm or similarity\(\). OpenSearch fuzzy queries use Levenshtein distance natively, with no extension required. Table bonus: +10 pattern match (once for the `approximate-match` group).
- ElastiCache, no: ElastiCache cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on ElastiCache.
- Aurora PostgreSQL, native, class score 80: pg\_trgm's similarity\(\), the % operator and the &lt;-&gt; distance are native once the extension is created, and a GIN or GiST trigram index serves them \(PostgreSQL documentation, pg\_trgm, Index Support\). Class score \(#728\): 80, an index serves the match.
- Aurora MySQL, no: Aurora MySQL cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### geospatial

Name: Geospatial query.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.redis_analysis_tools:analyze_redis_use_cases`.

- ElastiCache, fit (medium) (redis-geospatial-001): Detected geospatial query patterns
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### graph-traversal-hierarchy

Name: Graph traversal or hierarchy.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, anti 0.8 (documentdb-anti-04): Self-referential FKs or recursive queries. $graphLookup runs on DocumentDB 8.0 instance-based clusters, not on 5.0 or earlier and not on elastic clusters \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### group-concat-pivot

Name: Group concatenation or pivot.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_mysql_analysis_tools:detect_mysql_specific_features`, `src.tools.analysis.aurora_pg_analysis_tools:detect_pg_specific_features`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 75 (aurora-pg-10): String aggregation with string\_agg \(a source's GROUP\_CONCAT, STRING\_AGG or LISTAGG\) for pivoting and denormalized output, server-side \(PostgreSQL documentation, Aggregate Functions\). Table bonus: +5 pattern match. Counts toward the engine's feature complexity bonus.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 75 (aurora-mysql-04): String aggregation with GROUP\_CONCAT \(a source's STRING\_AGG or LISTAGG\) for pivoting and denormalized output, server-side \(MySQL Reference Manual, Aggregate Function Descriptions\). Table bonus: +5 pattern match. Counts toward the engine's feature complexity bonus.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### heavy-cross-collection-joins

Name: Heavy cross-collection joins.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, anti 0.6 (documentdb-anti-01): Queries joining 3 or more tables. Each join becomes a $lookup stage that reads the joined collection for the documents flowing through it, one stage per collection, with a nested-loop, hash or sort-merge algorithm \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Functional differences, $lookup\); correlated $lookup needs DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### high-frequency-pk-lookup

Name: High-frequency primary key lookup.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, anti 0.8 (aurora-anti-01): Single-row SELECT by primary key at very high frequency \(more than 30 calls/second\). Aurora serves it natively with a B-tree point read and scales reads with up to 15 Aurora Replicas \(Amazon Aurora User Guide, Replication with Amazon Aurora\).
- Aurora MySQL, anti 0.8 (aurora-anti-01): Single-row SELECT by primary key at very high frequency \(more than 30 calls/second\). Aurora serves it natively with a B-tree point read and scales reads with up to 15 Aurora Replicas \(Amazon Aurora User Guide, Replication with Amazon Aurora\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### high-frequency-small-updates

Name: High-frequency small updates.
No analysis reports this pattern today.
Writes only: no parity anchor borrows from it and no access class lists it.

- DocumentDB, anti 0.4 (documentdb-anti-03): Frequent updates to single fields of large documents. Catalog-only guidance with no detector: the documentation states no limit for it, so it costs nothing \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Best practices for Amazon DocumentDB\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### high-ingest

Name: High ingest.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.opensearch_analysis_tools:analyze_opensearch_use_cases`.
Writes only: no parity anchor borrows from it and no access class lists it.

- OpenSearch, fit 90 (os-07): High-throughput INSERT workload \(&gt;= 10 calls/second per table\). OpenSearch bulk indexing API is designed for sustained high-ingest. Auto-sharding and refresh interval tuning support this pattern. Table bonus: +15 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### high-volume-text-search

Name: High-volume text search.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, anti 0.7 (aurora-anti-07): High-frequency text search patterns \(LIKE '%', tsvector, ILIKE\) on a text-heavy table \(&gt;40% text columns\). A B-tree serves no leading-wildcard LIKE, so without a text or trigram index the search reads every row \(MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes; PostgreSQL documentation, pg\_trgm\).
- Aurora MySQL, anti 0.7 (aurora-anti-07): High-frequency text search patterns \(LIKE '%', tsvector, ILIKE\) on a text-heavy table \(&gt;40% text columns\). A B-tree serves no leading-wildcard LIKE, so without a text or trigram index the search reads every row \(MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes; PostgreSQL documentation, pg\_trgm\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### json-document-query

Name: JSON document query.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_mysql_analysis_tools:detect_mysql_specific_features`, `src.tools.analysis.aurora_pg_analysis_tools:detect_pg_specific_features`, `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, fit 80 (documentdb-06): A query that reads JSON paths \(JSON\_EXTRACT, -&gt;&gt;, JSON\_VALUE\): the data is already semi-structured, and each path maps to a document field. Table bonus: +8 pattern match.
- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 85 (aurora-pg-03): JSONB operations \(-&gt;&gt;, @&gt;, jsonb\_agg, jsonb\_build\_object\) for semi-structured data within relational context. Aurora PG provides GIN-indexed JSONB queries, combining document flexibility with relational joins. Table bonus: +10 pattern match.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 85 (aurora-mysql-01): JSON document queries using JSON\_EXTRACT, JSON\_CONTAINS, or -&gt;&gt; operator. Aurora MySQL 8.0+ provides multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays and generated columns for indexing JSON paths. Table bonus: +10 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### key-value-lookup

Name: Key-value lookup.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.dynamodb_analysis_tools:analyze_dynamodb_use_cases`, `src.tools.analysis.aurora_common_analysis_tools:analyze_aurora_common_use_cases`.

- DynamoDB, fit 100 (dynamodb-01): Single-item reads by the full primary key: GetItem, or BatchGetItem for up to 100 keys and 16 MB, at single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale \(Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Working with items; Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, BatchGetItem\). Table bonus: +15 pattern match.
- DocumentDB, -, class score 80 (parity anchor, from `key-value-lookup`): A single-document read by \_id or a unique index is a native indexed lookup; DocumentDB's analysis does not report the pattern and it adds no cross-engine penalty. Class score \(#728\): 80, parity anchor: no engine-specific evidence yet; the same B-tree point read Aurora's own key lookup is rated at \(key-value-lookup, 80\), until a measurement replaces it \(#936\).
- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 80 (aurora-common-12): A read of one row, or an IN-list batch, by its full primary or unique key: a B-tree index point read, served from memory once cached, with read replicas to scale the reads \(PostgreSQL documentation, Index Types; MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes\).
- Aurora MySQL, fit 80 (aurora-common-12): A read of one row, or an IN-list batch, by its full primary or unique key: a B-tree index point read, served from memory once cached, with read replicas to scale the reads \(PostgreSQL documentation, Index Types; MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes\).

### regex-search

Name: Regular expression search.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.opensearch_analysis_tools:analyze_opensearch_use_cases`.
Exemption note: {engine} runs this search pattern natively: not penalized. OpenSearch is worth the move only when traffic, data size or search depth justify a dedicated search engine

- DynamoDB, no: DynamoDB cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on DynamoDB.
- DocumentDB, native, class score 45: $regex is a native operator, but only a prefix regular expression without the i, m or o options uses an index; any other is a collection scan \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Query planner\). Class score \(#728\): 45, a scan of every document; a prefix regular expression is prefix-regex's \(#982\).
- OpenSearch, fit 75 (os-03): Regex pattern matching \(REGEXP, RLIKE, PostgreSQL ~ operator\). OpenSearch supports regexp queries with finite automaton execution, avoiding full-scan overhead. Table bonus: +5 pattern match.
- ElastiCache, no: ElastiCache cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on ElastiCache.
- Aurora PostgreSQL, native, class score 75: The ~ and ~\* operators are native SQL, and a pg\_trgm GIN or GiST index serves them as far as trigrams can be extracted from the expression; one with none reads the whole index \(PostgreSQL documentation, pg\_trgm, Index Support\). Class score \(#728\): 75, index-assisted, less reliably than a LIKE.
- Aurora MySQL, native, class score 45: REGEXP and RLIKE are native SQL, but they are not among the comparisons a B-tree index serves, so every row is read and tested \(MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes\). Class score \(#728\): 45, a scan of every row.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### secondary-attribute-filter

Name: Secondary attribute filter.
No analysis reports this pattern today.

- DocumentDB, -, class score 75 (parity anchor, from `secondary-attribute-filter`): Filters on any field, served by single-field and compound secondary indexes, are native queries. Class score \(#728\): 75, parity anchor: no engine-specific evidence yet; the secondary-index filter Aurora is rated at for this class \(secondary-attribute-filter, 75\), until a measurement replaces it \(#936\).
- OpenSearch, -, class score 75 (parity anchor, from `secondary-attribute-filter`): Every field is indexed \(inverted index, BKD trees, doc values\), so a multi-attribute filter is a native filter-context query; reads only, near real time, and never a write \(not a system of record\). Class score \(#728\): 75, parity anchor: no engine-specific evidence yet; the rating Aurora has for this class \(secondary-attribute-filter, 75\), until a measurement replaces it \(#936\).
- Aurora PostgreSQL, -, class score 75: A WHERE clause on non-key columns is native SQL: a B-tree index range scan on an indexed column, and a bitmap scan that combines several indexes with AND and OR \(PostgreSQL documentation, Combining Multiple Indexes\). Class score \(#728\): 75, a read served by secondary indexes; unmeasured \(#936\).
- Aurora MySQL, -, class score 75: A WHERE clause on non-key columns is native SQL: a range access on an indexed column, and an index merge that combines range scans of several indexes of one table \(MySQL Reference Manual, Index Merge Optimization\). Class score \(#728\): 75, a read served by secondary indexes; unmeasured \(#936\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### substring-match

Name: Substring match.
Detected by `src.agents.referee.substring_match:substring_matches`.
Scan threshold: 1 calls per second and 100,000 table rows, both reached. A leading-wildcard LIKE, or a regular expression, reads every row of the table on an engine with no index for it \(MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes: a B-tree serves LIKE only for a constant pattern that does not start with a wildcard, and no REGEXP\). At 1 call per second on 100,000 rows that is 100,000 rows read every second, the point where the analysis cost bands \(src/tools/analysis/scoring.py\) stop calling a query rare and a table small; below either, the scan is cheap enough to keep.

- DocumentDB, scan: runs a leading-wildcard LIKE, and a regular expression that is not a case-sensitive prefix, as an unanchored $regex, which reads every document \(the query planner uses an index only for a prefix $regex without the i, m or o options\); a text index serves word search with $text. Word search: create a text index on the field and query it with $text, which serves word search.
- OpenSearch, native: serves a leading-wildcard match natively, with wildcard queries or an n-gram analyzer on the field, and a regular expression with a regexp query.
- Aurora PostgreSQL, native: indexes a leading-wildcard LIKE and a regular expression with a pg\_trgm trigram index \(GIN or GiST\), an extension to create \(the PostgreSQL documentation of pg\_trgm describes its index support for LIKE, ILIKE, ~ and ~\*\). Word search: create the pg\_trgm extension and a GIN trigram index on the column \(CREATE EXTENSION pg\_trgm\), which serves this LIKE, word searches included; full-text search \(to\_tsvector\) also ranks word matches.
- Aurora MySQL, scan: scans a leading-wildcard LIKE and a REGEXP: FULLTEXT indexes are word-based and serve MATCH ... AGAINST, never LIKE \(MySQL Reference Manual, Full-Text Search Functions\), and no index serves REGEXP. Word search: rewrite it as MATCH ... AGAINST over a FULLTEXT index on the column, which serves word search.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, anti 0.4 (aurora-anti-04): Append-only table: 10 or more INSERTs per second, no other writes \(no UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE or REPLACE\) and reads under 1% of its calls, so rows accumulate unread and the table grows without bound unless old rows expire. Guidance only: Aurora sustains the rate, and dropping old partitions is a data-lifecycle task \(PostgreSQL documentation, Table Partitioning\).
- Aurora MySQL, anti 0.4 (aurora-anti-04): Append-only table: 10 or more INSERTs per second, no other writes \(no UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE or REPLACE\) and reads under 1% of its calls, so rows accumulate unread and the table grows without bound unless old rows expire. Guidance only: Aurora sustains the rate, and dropping old partitions is a data-lifecycle task \(PostgreSQL documentation, Table Partitioning\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### upsert-conflict

Name: Upsert on conflict.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_pg_analysis_tools:detect_pg_specific_features`.
Writes only: no parity anchor borrows from it and no access class lists it.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 80 (aurora-pg-07): UPSERT with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and RETURNING clause. Aurora PG handles atomic insert-or-update in a single statement with row-level locking, with no read-modify-write cycle needed. Table bonus: +5 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### upsert-duplicate-key

Name: Upsert on duplicate key.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_mysql_analysis_tools:detect_mysql_specific_features`.
Writes only: no parity anchor borrows from it and no access class lists it.

- Aurora MySQL, fit 80 (aurora-mysql-03): UPSERT using INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. Aurora MySQL handles atomic insert-or-update with row-level locking on the unique/primary key. Table bonus: +5 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### variant-attributes

Name: Variant attributes.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, fit 80 (documentdb-01): An entity whose attribute set varies \(by type or category, or as attribute rows\), read by its key: DocumentDB stores each entity as one document of up to 16 MB with only the fields it has; it has no wildcard index, so each queried attribute needs its own index \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Quotas and limits; Functional differences\). Table bonus: +10 pattern match.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### wide-transaction

Name: Wide transaction.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.dynamodb_analysis_tools:analyze_dynamodb_use_cases`.
Penalty: 10 (`bounded_limit`). DynamoDB runs every item of a wider write within a documented bound: one PartiQL DELETE or UPDATE changes one item \(its condition resolves to a single primary key\), and the documented way to change several is a transaction of up to 100 items or a batch \(Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, PartiQL delete statements; Amazon DynamoDB Transactions\), so the design splits the write into bounded calls, reads the keys of a predicate-picked set first, and gives up all-or-nothing atomicity across the calls; the data model needs no redesign \(needs\_redesign is for an access path no server-side operation serves\).
Writes only: no parity anchor borrows from it and no access class lists it.

- DynamoDB, anti 0.3 (dynamodb-ap-04): A write wider than one transaction: more than 100 items, or rows a range, join, subquery or a filter with no key anchor picks \(a write by a non-unique key column is a key-scoped Query plus batch write, not this\). DynamoDB TransactWriteItems holds up to 100 items and 4 MB across tables \(Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Amazon DynamoDB Transactions\).
- No effect on: DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### wildcard-search

Name: Wildcard search.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.opensearch_analysis_tools:analyze_opensearch_use_cases`.
Exemption note: {engine} runs this search pattern natively: not penalized. OpenSearch is worth the move only when traffic, data size or search depth justify a dedicated search engine

- DynamoDB, no: DynamoDB cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on DynamoDB.
- DocumentDB, native, class score 45: $regex expresses LIKE natively, but only a prefix regular expression without the i, m or o options uses an index, so a leading wildcard is a collection scan \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Query planner\). Class score \(#728\): 45, a scan of every document; what the scan costs a frequent query on a large table stays substring-match's penalty \(#493\).
- OpenSearch, fit 80 (os-02): LIKE/ILIKE wildcard queries on text columns. OpenSearch wildcard queries are more scalable than SQL LIKE on large datasets, with no full-table scan. Table bonus: +10 pattern match (once for the `approximate-match` group).
- ElastiCache, no: ElastiCache cannot run this pattern: a query another engine reports it for loses 40 points on ElastiCache.
- Aurora PostgreSQL, native, class score 80: LIKE and ILIKE are native SQL, and a pg\_trgm GIN or GiST index serves them with a leading wildcard too, an extension to create \(PostgreSQL documentation, pg\_trgm, Index Support; the substring-match pattern, #493\). Class score \(#728\): 80, an index serves the match.
- Aurora MySQL, native, class score 45: LIKE is native SQL, but a B-tree index serves LIKE only when the pattern does not start with a wildcard and a FULLTEXT index serves only MATCH ... AGAINST, so a leading wildcard reads every row \(MySQL Reference Manual, Comparison of B-Tree and Hash Indexes\). Class score \(#728\): 45, a scan of every row; what the scan costs a frequent query on a large table stays substring-match's penalty \(#493\).
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### window-function

Name: Window function.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.aurora_pg_analysis_tools:detect_pg_specific_features`, `src.tools.analysis.aurora_mysql_analysis_tools:detect_mysql_specific_features`.

- Aurora PostgreSQL, fit 90 (aurora-pg-02): Window functions \(OVER, PARTITION BY, ROW\_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD\) for running totals, rankings and row-level analytics, in one pass without self-joins, with the ROWS, RANGE and GROUPS frame modes and frame exclusion \(PostgreSQL documentation, Window Function Calls\). Table bonus: +10 pattern match. Counts toward the engine's feature complexity bonus.
- Aurora MySQL, fit 85 (aurora-mysql-07): Window functions \(OVER, PARTITION BY, ROW\_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD\) for running totals, rankings and row-level analytics, in one pass without self-joins, on MySQL 8.0, which Aurora MySQL version 3 is compatible with; MySQL documents fewer frame features \(no DISTINCT in a windowed aggregate, no nested window functions, no frame bounds that depend on the current row: MySQL Reference Manual, Window Function Restrictions\). Table bonus: +10 pattern match. Counts toward the engine's feature complexity bonus.
- No effect on: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

### window-functions

Name: Window functions in a document pipeline.
Detected by `src.tools.analysis.documentdb_analysis_tools:analyze_documentdb_use_cases`.

- DocumentDB, anti 0.5 (documentdb-anti-07): SQL window functions $setWindowFields serves \(ROW\_NUMBER, RANK, running totals\): DocumentDB 8.0.2 or later on an instance-based cluster. LAG and LEAD \($shift\) and NTILE \(no bucketing window operator\) run on no version, so they are a hard capability gap, not this entry \(Amazon DocumentDB Developer Guide, Supported MongoDB APIs, operations, and data types\).
- No effect on: DynamoDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache, Aurora PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL.
- Not modelled yet (future enhancement): Neptune, Keyspaces.

Table bonus: +8 pattern match.
